locator.work: Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (with The English Physician Enlarged), new edn. 1850 — Project Gutenberg eBook #49513, public domain
locator.heading: Lettuce

source_text:
IT is so well known, being generally used as a Sallad-herb, that it is
altogether needless to write any description thereof.

_Government and virtues._] The Moon owns them, and that is the reason
they cool and moisten what heat and dryness Mars causeth, because Mars
has his fall in Cancer; and they cool the heat because the Sun rules
it, between whom and the Moon is a reception in the generation of men,
as you may see in my Guide for Women. The juice of Lettuce mixed or
boiled with Oil of Roses, applied to the forehead and temples procures
sleep, and eases the headache proceeding of an hot cause: Being eaten
boiled, it helps to loosen the belly. It helps digestion, quenches
thirst, increases milk in nurses, eases griping pains in the stomach
or bowels, that come of choler. Applied outwardly to the region of the
heart, liver or reins, or by bathing the said places with the juice
of distilled water, wherein some white Sanders, or red Roses are put;
not only represses the heat and inflammations therein, but comforts
and strengthens those parts, and also tempers the heat of urine. Galen
advises old men to use it with spice; and where spices are wanting,
to add Mints, Rochet, and such like hot herbs, or else Citron Lemon,
or Orange seeds, to abate the cold of one and heat of the other. The
seed and distilled water of the Lettuce work the same effects in all
things; but the use of Lettuce is chiefly forbidden to those that are
short-winded, or have any imperfection in the lungs, or spit blood.

evidence.summary: No EMA monograph found. Retrieved PubMed articles address contact allergy, environmental microplastics, and agricultural biostimulants; none provide clinical evidence supporting traditional uses for stomach pain, insomnia, or inflammation.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence (PMID: 26289653) flags contact allergy risks, contradicting safety for internal use. No clinical trials support historical claims; only preclinical cooling properties offer partial plausibility.
concordance.uncertainty: High due to lack of modern clinical data and presence of specific allergen warnings in literature.

issues: Unearned Grade: The entry assigns a 'C' grade citing 'Modern evidence (PMID: 26289653)' for contact allergy risks. However, the evidence list shows `ema: false` and `pubmed_n: 3`, indicating a severe lack of clinical trials or EMA approval supporting any therapeutic efficacy or safety profile beyond basic botanical description. A 'C' grade implies some level of validated partial support, but with only 3 PubMed hits (likely non-clinical or general toxicity) and explicit warnings of allergy, the evidence base is insufficient to justify even a low-grade therapeutic claim without clear distinction between 'harmful' and 'ineffective'. The rationale claims 'partial plausibility' for cooling properties, yet no specific clinical evidence supports this mechanism in humans. This constitutes an unearned grade due to lack of efficacy/safety proof.
